w: On a hill called Salvokop stands a memorial that refuses to pick a single conflict to mourn - names from the South African Wars, both World Wars and the apartheid era are carved in together, one long reckoning with the country's fighting history inside a single park.
s: One memorial, every war South Africa fought
_facts: Park on Salvokop in Pretoria
Includes a memorial listing those killed in the South African Wars, WWI, WWII and the apartheid era

w: Paul Kruger laid the cornerstone himself in 1889, and for over a decade this Renaissance Revival hall on Church Square housed the Volksraad, parliament of the old South African Republic. The Transvaal Museum briefly squatted upstairs; then came the Boer War, annexation, and a quiet retirement as a heritage site.
s: Kruger's parliament, retired to Church Square
_facts: Housed the Volksraad, parliament of the South African Republic, 1891-1902
Designed by Sytze Wierda in Renaissance Revival style; cornerstone laid 6 May 1889 by President Paul Kruger, completed December 1891
Transvaal Museum briefly occupied its upper floor from 1892 before relocating
Building became vacant after the 1902 British annexation ended the Volksraad; declared a Provincial Heritage Site in 1999

w: Across the street from Burgers Park sits this stately mansion, now kept as a house museum - one of Pretoria's rare chances to walk through grand domestic architecture instead of just admiring it from the pavement, room by room rather than through a fence.
s: A stately mansion turned museum, by the park
_facts: Stately mansion and museum located opposite Burgers Park in Pretoria

w: Laid out in 1946 across 76 hectares in Brummeria, this is one of South Africa's nine National Botanical Gardens, its paths climbing a rocky ridge that splits the grounds east to west. These days it also quietly hosts the headquarters of the South African National Biodiversity Institute.
_facts: One of South Africa's nine National Botanical Gardens
76 hectares in Brummeria, eastern Pretoria, flanking a central rocky ridge; established 1946
Hosts the headquarters of the South African National Biodiversity Institute

w: Built in 1884 for Boer president Paul Kruger, this house was mixed with milk instead of water when the available cement proved too poor - and wired for electricity before most of Pretoria had it. Two stone lions still guard the verandah, a birthday gift from mining magnate Barney Barnato in 1896.
s: Built with milk in the cement, guarded by lions
_facts: Residence of Paul Kruger, built 1884 by architect Tom Claridge and builder Charles Clark
Milk was used instead of water for mixing the cement, due to poor available cement quality
One of the first houses in Pretoria lit by electricity
Two stone lions on the verandah, a birthday gift from Barney Barnato on 10 October 1896
Now a house museum recreating the period Kruger lived in

n: Statue of Nelson Mandela, Union Buildings
w: Nine metres tall and unveiled on the Day of Reconciliation, 16 December 2013, this statue on the Union Buildings lawn closed out ten days of official mourning that followed Nelson Mandela's death eleven days earlier. A single bronze figure, arms open, doing the work of a nation's goodbye.
s: Nine metres of Mandela on the Union Buildings lawn
_facts: 9-metre statue of Nelson Mandela on the Union Buildings grounds
Unveiled on the Day of Reconciliation, 16 December 2013, closing the official ten-day mourning period after Mandela's death on 5 December 2013

w: Named for the Wonderboom - Afrikaans for 'marvel tree' - that still stands near the entrance, this 200-hectare reserve climbs the Magaliesberg ridge to a derelict fort built during the Second Boer War. The paved walkway up is steep, but the ruins at the top open onto sweeping views over the whole city.
s: A 'marvel tree' guarded by a ruined Boer War fort
_facts: 200-hectare reserve incorporating part of the Magaliesberg range in northern Pretoria
Main attractions are the Wonderboom ('marvel tree') and the derelict Fort Wonderboompoort, built late 19th century during the Second Boer War
Fort ruins reached by a steep paved walkway and afford sweeping views of the city
Area declared a reserve on 28 December 1949

n: Ditsong National Museum of Cultural History
w: Part of the Ditsong network that also runs Pretoria's natural-history and art collections nearby, this one keeps its brief narrow: the stages and forms of culture across South Africa, one gallery at a time, under the same shared branding as its sister museums.
s: South Africa's culture, under one Ditsong roof
_facts: Museum showcasing the various stages and forms of culture in South Africa
Part of the Ditsong Museums of South Africa network, located in Pretoria

w: Built in 1978 to carry microwave and mobile signals across the city, this Muckleneuk Hill tower comes with an observation deck for the rest of us. Between 2009 and 2012 it also wore a 24-metre fibreglass soccer ball, eight storeys tall, in honour of the World Cup its sponsor was busy branding.
s: A telecoms tower that once wore a giant soccer ball
_facts: Formerly the John Vorster Tower; built 1978 on Muckleneuk Hill in the Lukasrand suburb
Primary purpose is wireless telecommunications; features an observation deck; branded for Telkom SA
From September 2009 to 2012 it carried a 24-metre, eight-storey fibreglass soccer ball for the 2010 World Cup

w: Raised in 1877 in full Gothic dress on Bosman Street, this church only became a cathedral in name in 1948, then the seat of the Archdiocese of Pretoria in 1951 under a bull issued by Pope Pius XII. Seven decades of parish life, then a paperwork promotion to match the title everyone already used.
s: Gothic on Bosman Street, cathedral since 1948
_facts: Catholic cathedral in Bosman Street, Pretoria; built 1877 in Gothic architectural style
Cathedral dignity since 1948; became seat of the Metropolitan Archdiocese of Pretoria in 1951, created by the bull Suprema Nobis of Pope Pius XII

n: Ditsong National Museum of Natural History
w: Established in 1895 by the old South African Republic as the Transvaal Museum, this Paul Kruger Street building sits directly across from Pretoria's City Hall and has been cataloguing the country's natural history since before the Union of South Africa existed. Renamed, not replaced, in 2010.
s: The old Transvaal Museum, cataloguing since 1895
_facts: Formerly the Transvaal Museum; on Paul Kruger Street, between Visagie and Minnaar Streets, opposite Pretoria City Hall
Established 1895 by the former South African Republic (Transvaal)
Became a founding museum of Ditsong Museums of South Africa in 2010

n: National Zoological Garden of South Africa
w: J. W. B. Gunning founded this 80-hectare zoo in 1899, and it has since grown into one of the eight largest zoos on the planet - South Africa's official national collection, sprawling through the middle of Pretoria rather than tucked away on the edge of town.
_facts: 80-hectare national zoo of South Africa, founded by J. W. B. Gunning in 1899
One of the eight largest zoos in the world

w: Paul Kruger laid the foundation stone in 1897 for what became the Gauteng High Court - and, decades later, the courtroom for the Rivonia Trial, where Nelson Mandela and his co-accused were tried for treason and sent to prison for what turned into a generation. Same square as the Ou Raadsaal, opposite fates.
s: Where the Rivonia Trial put Mandela on trial
_facts: Forms part of the northern facade of Church Square; designed by Sytze Wierda; foundation stone laid 8 June 1897 by President Paul Kruger
Headquarters of the Gauteng Division of the High Court of South Africa
Site of the Rivonia Trial, where Nelson Mandela and other ANC members were charged with treason and jailed

w: A 1932 bequest from Lady Michaelis, mourning her husband Sir Max, gave this Arcadia gallery its first windfall of Dutch Old Masters - but the museum's real project became building out South African art instead, from Pierneef and Irma Stern to Lucas Sithole, whose unfinished work arrived here after his 1994 death.
s: A whole city block of South African art
_facts: Art gallery in Arcadia, Pretoria, occupying a full city block; houses the City Council's art collection built up since the 1930s
1932 bequest from Lady Michaelis of 17th-century North Dutch school works, after the death of her husband Sir Max Michaelis
South African works include Pierneef, Wenning, Oerder, Anton van Wouw and Irma Stern
After sculptor Lucas Sithole's death in 1994, half his unfinished work was donated to the museum via the Haenggi Foundation
